title: Kinetics of multistate DNA polymerases
abstract: In the present paper, we apply the iterative mathematical method previously developed for the kinetics of template-directed multistate copolymerization to the kinetics of DNA replication by polymerases having multiple structural states. In particular, we study a two-state kinetic model for the T7 DNA polymerase. We obtain the mean velocity for the growth of the copy along the template, the error probability of DNA replication by the polymerase, and the local probabilities of base-pair formation along the template sequence. Furthermore, we show that the iterative method is more than a million times faster than usual numerical simulation methods. Results are also obtained in the approximation of homogenization of template heterogeneities.
summary: This work develops advanced mathematical methods to calculate the kinetics of DNA replication by polymerases with multiple structural states. By applying iterative techniques to master equations, the authors derive exact formulas for key metrics like growth speed and error rate. This provides a powerful theoretical tool for analyzing complex biochemical processes far exceeding standard numerical simulation capabilities.
main_problem: The paper investigates the kinetics of DNA replication catalyzed by polymerases that exhibit multiple structural states.
main_result: Exact analytical solutions for growth velocity and error probability are derived using iterative mathematical methods, which prove significantly faster than direct numerical simulations.
method: The core method involves applying an iterative mathematical technique to solve the coupled master equations governing the system's time evolution in the long-time limit.
model_or_system: The model uses a two-state kinetic framework (E and F) for T7 DNA polymerase acting on a template sequence, governed by rate constants derived from a reversible reaction network.
key_observables: Mean velocity of copy growth ($v$), error probability ($\eta$), local probabilities of base-pair formation ($\mu(m; l)$), and mean local dwell time ($	au_l$).
important_parameters: Nucleotide concentrations (e.g., $10^{-3}$ M), rate constants ($k$), and the structural states (E, F).
main_assumptions: Key approximations include assuming quasi-equilibrium for nucleotide binding/unbinding (Michaelis-Menten kinetics) and using homogenization to simplify template heterogeneities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how local probabilities and dwell times vary with template sequence composition under different nucleotide concentration regimes, confirming expected pairing dominance.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the full kinetic master equations to simplifying them via quasi-equilibrium assumptions. It then develops iterative matrix methods to find exact asymptotic solutions for observables like velocity and error rate, comparing these results against numerical simulations.
why_interesting: While focused on biochemistry, the rigorous application of master equation reduction techniques, steady-state analysis (e.g., IFS), and comparison between analytical/numerical approaches mirrors methodologies used in analyzing open quantum systems or reaction-diffusion processes where complex state spaces must be simplified.

E denotes the open state of the polymerase, F its closed state, {mj} the nucleotide units composing the copy, {nj} those of the template, {mjP} the molecules of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate, and P the molecules of inorganic pyrophosphate. The rates of the reactions are explained in the text.

FIG. 2: Representation of the kinetic scheme of Fig. 1 after its reduction using the assumptions (2) of a Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics for the DNA polymerase. This reduced scheme corresponds to the kinetic equations (3) and (4), which are deduced in Appendix A. The notations are the same as in Fig. 1. The transition rates are given by Eqs. (6)-(9).

The lines are those of theory using the formulas (41) for the velocity and (44) for the error probability with Nloop = 10.
